documents.title: Tokyo Guidelines 2018 Diagnostic Criteria and Severity Grading of Acute Cholecystitis

chunks.content: Introduction With the progression of societal aging, the proportion of individuals aged 80 and above seeking medical services has gradually increased in clinical practice— a demographic shift that amplifies the clinical challenges posed by diseases like acute calculous cholecystitis (ACC) [ ]. Early laparoscopic cholecystectomy (ELC) has been recommended as the preferred therapeutic option for young and otherwise fit ACC patients by the World Society of Emergency Surgery (WSES) and the Tokyo Guidelines 2018 (TG18) [ , ]. However, the guidelines do not provide sufficient information about the safety and efficacy of surgery in patients with old age, especially those who were unsuitable for surgery initially. In the older population who received LC, studies have also reported that patients aged ≥ 80 years had higher conversion rate, longer length of hospital stay, and longer operation time than those aged 65–79 years or those younger than 65 years due to chronic scarring and inflammation around the gallbladder [ , ]. This elevated risk stems from age-related physiological declines, including reduced organ reserve and weakened immune function, coupled with atypical clinical presentations (35% of octogenarians lack classic symptoms like right upper quadrant pain or fever) and a high burden of comorbidities such as hypertension and diabetes. Elderly patients are predisposed to elevated risks of perioperative complications and mortality, primarily attributable to the presence of comorbid conditions and impaired physiological reserve. A majority of clinicians advocate that ultrasound-guided percutaneous transhepatic gallbladder drainage (PTGBD) or non-surgical management strategies represent more favorable options for this population, given that such modalities effectively obviate complications stemming from surgical procedures [ ]. However, high-quality clinical data to back up this management approach is currently lacking . The present study was designed to assess the efficacy of ELC versus PTGBD in elderly patients with ACC. Findings from this research are expected to yield valuable insights for guiding clinical decision-making in the geriatric demographic. Materials and methods‌ General information‌ This was a retrospective cohort study that include 174 elderly patients (≥80 years old) with ACC who underwent surgical therapy between July 2018 and June 2025. According to the treatment modality, the patients were divided into two groups: the‌ early laparoscopic cholecystectomy (E‌LC) group (n=121) and the percutaneous transhepatic gallbladder drainage (PTGBD) Group (n=53). For the purpose of this study, ELC was defined as LC performed with a time interval of ≤7 days from the onset of symptoms to surgical intervention. The study was approved by the Ethics Committee of Zhejiang Hospital(Approval No. ZJHIRB-2025–178 K)and conducted in compliance with the Declaration of Helsinki. The diagnostic criteria for ACC are as follows based on Tokyo Guidelines 2018 [ ]. Imaging tests suggested signs of gallbladder inflammation. Preoperative evaluations included complete blood count + C-reactive protein (CRP), urinalysis, stool analysis, biochemical profiles, coagulation function, tumor markers, hepatitis B serology + pre-S1 antigen, pre-transfusion testing, chest computed tomography (CT), electrocardiogram, hepatobiliary ultrasound, and Magnetic Resonance Cholangiopancreatography (MRCP). General patient data and perioperative outcomes (e.g., complications, recovery) were collected and analyzed. ‌Inclusion criteria‌:Age ≥ 80 years; ACC treated with PTGBD or ELC. ‌Exclusion criteria‌:Incomplete medical records; Concurrent choledocholithiasis or intrahepatic bile duct stones. Surgical methods‌ Laparoscopic surgery‌ The “3-port” or “4-port” approach was employed. A 10-mm Trocar (Kangji, Hangzhou) was placed 1 cm below the umbilicus as the observation port, connected to an insufflator to maintain pneumoperitoneum at 14 mmHg. After laparoscope insertion, the abdominal cavity was inspected, and additional Trocars were positioned based on intra-abdominal space availability: typically 2 cm below the xiphoid process and 5 cm below the right costal margin at the midclavicular line. The “4-port” method added a 5-mm Trocar 5 cm lateral to the right umbilicus. In cases of severe edema or adhesions in Calot’s triangle, a retrograde cholecystectomy was performed. After gallbladder mobilization, tissues in Calot’s triangle were carefully dissected. Blunt dissection with suction irrigation was used to identify the cystic artery and duct when tissues were edematous but pliable. For “frozen-like” fibrotic tissues, laparoscopic forceps were employed for meticulous separation without forceful manipulation. No routine drainage was placed. Percutaneous transhepatic gallbladder drainage Ultrasound-guided gallbladder localization was performed to select the optimal puncture site, avoiding hepatic vessels and bile ducts. Under real-time ultrasound guidance, a puncture needle was inserted percutaneously into the gallbladder. A guidewire was advanced through the needle, followed by placement of a drainage catheter over the guidewire, connected to a drainage bag. The initial bile drainage volume and bile characteristics (clear, turbid, purulent) were recorded, and routine bile bacterial culture was performed. Evaluation criteria for drainage efficacy: Effective drainage was defined as a bile drainage volume of ≥ 100 ml within 24 h after operation, accompanied by improved bile characteristics (turbid/purulent bile turning clear or significantly alleviated). The initial bile drainage volume and bile characteristics (clear, turbid, purulent) were recorded, and routine bile bacterial culture was performed. Evaluation criteria for drainage efficacy: Effective drainage was defined as a bile drainage volume of ≥ 100 ml within 24 h after operation, accompanied by improved bile characteristics (turbid/purulent bile turning clear or significantly alleviated). Ineffective drainage was defined as a drainage volume of < 100 ml, no bile drainage, or no improvement in bile characteristics. Criteria for Initiation of Postoperative Ambulation Standardized criteria were established for the initiation of postoperative ambulation in our department. All of the following conditions must be satisfied simultaneously: Stable vital signs (body temperature < 38.5℃, heart rate 60–100 beats/min, blood pressure 90–140/60–90 mmHg, respiratory rate 12–20 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation ≥ 95% without supplemental oxygen); No obvious abdominal pain or distension, with a Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) pain score ≤ 3; No early postoperative complications such as active bleeding or bile leakage; Clear consciousness and normal limb movement, with the ability to cooperate in basic maneuvers including sitting up and standing. Once the above criteria were met, patients were instructed to perform ambulation gradually under the guidance of primary nurses. The duration of the first ambulation was limited to 5–10 min and was increased progressively according to individual tolerance. Criteria for complications grading The Clavien-Dindo classification system was used to grade complications in both groups, with the specific grading criteria as follows: Grade I: Minor complications that did not require medical or surgical intervention. Grade II: Complications that required medical treatment (e.g., antibiotics). Grade III: Complications that necessitated surgical or interventional intervention. Grade IV: Life-threatening severe complications (e.g., septic shock, severe organ failure). Grade V: Death. Diagnostic criteria of complications Catheter-related infection: Erythema, warmth, tenderness and purulent exudation at the catheter entry site. Bile leakage: Ultrasonographically detected hypoechoic fluid collection around the liver or gallbladder surgical field, with bile drained via ultrasound-guided percutaneous puncture. Incisional infection: Erythema, warmth, tenderness and purulent exudation at the surgical incision site. Intra-abdominal infection: Upper abdominal pain with exudative changes in the gallbladder surgical field on abdominal CT, combined with positive bile bacterial culture during the index hospitalization. Acute cerebral infarction: Limb hemiplegia or facial palsy, with cerebral infarction confirmed by cranial CT and MRI. Intra-abdominal hemorrhage: Ultrasonographically detected hypoechoic fluid collection around the liver and gallbladder surgical field, with hemorrhagic fluid drained via ultrasound-guided percutaneous puncture. Detailed management measures for complications Accidental catheter dislodgement (PTGBD group): Patients were comprehensively evaluated for abdominal symptoms, vital signs and inflammatory indicators. Re-PTGBD was performed for those with recurrent pain, fever or elevated inflammation; asymptomatic patients received conservative treatment with close observation. Catheter obstruction (PTGBD group): The catheter was pulsatile-flushed with 30-50 mL normal saline. Continuous closed drainage was maintained if obstruction resolved (with daily patency monitoring); re-PTGBD was considered for unresolved obstruction based on symptom severity and inflammatory response. Catheter-related infection (PTGBD group): Daily iodophor disinfection, debridement and sterile dressing change were performed at the catheter entry site. Systemic antibiotics were not used for localized mild infection, with close monitoring for progression. Incisional infection (LC group): Superficial debridement was performed to remove purulent exudate, followed by daily iodophor disinfection and sterile dressing change. The incision was kept dry, and suture removal was delayed based on healing status. Bile leakage (PTGBD/LC group): Ultrasound-guided percutaneous puncture and drainage were performed for continuous bile drainage. Broad-spectrum systemic antibiotics were initiated to prevent secondary infection, with close monitoring of drainage volume and clinical symptoms until leakage resolved. Intra-abdominal infection (LC group): Intravenous targeted antibiotics were administered per bile culture sensitivity results. The antibiotic course (minimum 7–10 days for mild infection) was adjusted based on symptom improvement, vital signs and inflammatory indicators (CRP, WBC). Acute cerebral infarction (LC group): Patients were immediately transferred to neurology for standardized management (antiplatelet, lipid-lowering, neuroprotective therapy). Early individualized rehabilitation (limb, facial nerve training) was initiated after vital sign stabilization, with regular neurological assessment during follow-up. Intra-abdominal hemorrhage (LC group): Emergency ultrasound-guided puncture and drainage were performed to evacuate hemorrhagic fluid. Intravenous hemostatic agents were administered, with close monitoring of vital signs and hemoglobin. Broad-spectrum antibiotics were used for prophylaxis, and blood transfusion was given for severe anemia if needed. WBC and CRP were extracted from medical records, nursing documentation, and clinical laboratory results. Postoperative outcomes included time to ambulation, time to first flatus, postoperative fasting duration, postoperative hospital stay, and complications. The Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) was adopted for pain assessment, with VAS scores recorded for both groups on the first day postoperatively. For the PTGBD group, additional drainage-related indicators were collected, including initial bile drainage volume, bile characteristics, results of bile bacterial culture, patency rate of the drainage tube, and timing of tube removal. For long-term follow-up indicators, telephone follow-up and review of electronic medical records were conducted to collect data on the recurrence rate of the disease within 6 months after operation, as well as the incidence of long-term complications such as catheter-related complications (infection, obstruction, displacement), biliary stricture, and chronic abdominal pain. Propensity Score Matching (PSM) To control for confounding factors, PSM was used to balance the baseline characteristics between the two groups. Propensity scores were calculated using logistic regression with age, gender, ASA classification, CCI, BMI, history of hypertension, history of diabetes, smoking history, drinking history, WBC and CRP before surgery, and history of abdominal surgery as covariates. Nearest neighbor matching with a caliper width of 0.2 was applied at a 1:1 ratio for matching. Statistical analysis‌ Data analysis was performed using SPSS 20.0 (IBM Ltd., Armonk, NY) and R 3.53. Continuous variables were assessed for normality. Normally distributed data are presented as mean ± standard deviation (𝑥̅ ± SD) and analyzed using the Student’s t-test. Non-normally distributed data are summarized as median (interquartile range) [M (IQR)] and analyzed using the Mann-Whitney U test. Categorical variables are expressed as frequencies and percentages. Group comparisons for categorical data were performed using the chi-square (χ²) test or Fisher’s exact test. A P-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Results‌ Comparison of baseline characteristics before PSM Before matching, there were 121 patients in the ELC group and 53 patients in the PTGBD group. Statistically significant differences were observed between the two groups in ASA classification, history of diabetes, history of abdominal surgery, and WBC ( p < 0.05). Specifically, patients with ASA Grade IV accounted for 26.4% in the PTGBD group, while no such patients were present in the ELC group (Table ), reflecting the real clinical decision-making differences (ASA Grade IV is generally regarded as a contraindication for surgery), this study limited the comparison to patients with ASA Grades I-III. Results of PSM After excluding 14 patients with ASA Grade IV from the PTGBD group, 1:1 PSM was performed between the remaining 39 PTGBD patients and 121 ELC patients, and 39 matched pairs were successfully obtained. After matching, no statistically significant differences were observed between the two groups in age, gender, ASA classification (Grades I–III), CCI, BMI, WBC, CRP or any comorbidities and lifestyle factors (all p > 0.05). All standardized mean differences (SMD) were less than 0.25, indicating effective balance of baseline characteristics (Table ). Subgroup Analysis (High-Risk Patients with ASA Grade ≥ 4 in PTGBD): Among the 14 enrolled patients, there were 8 males and 6 females, with a mean age of 89.14 ± 5.01 years and a Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI) of 12.43 ± 2.38. The success rate of PTGBD was 100%, the overall complication rate was 28.6% (4/14), including 2 cases of Grade I complications (accidental catheter dislodgement), 1 case of Grade II complications (catheter-related infection) and 1 case of Grade III complications (bile leakage). The average length of hospital stay was 14.43 ± 2.68 days. Sensitivity analysis To verify the robustness of the PSM results, a series of sensitivity analyses were conducted. After adopting different matching ratios (1:2, 1:3), adjusting caliper widths (0.1, 0.3), using alternative matching methods (optimal matching), or excluding extreme cases, the baseline characteristics after matching remained well balanced (SMD < 0.25 and p > 0.05 for all key covariates). These findings confirmed that the main results of this study were insensitive to the selection of matching parameters and thus robust and reliable. With the delay of surgical timing, the operation time and intraoperative blood loss gradually increased, and the complication rate slightly elevated, but these differences were not statistically significant (all p > 0.05). Analysis of drainage efficacy in the PTGBD group: Effective drainage was achieved in 32 patients (82.1%), and ineffective drainage was observed in 7 patients (17.9%). The effective drainage subgroup showed significantly greater reduction in postoperative infection indicators and more obvious improvement in clinical symptoms compared with the ineffective drainage subgroup ( p < 0.05). The complication rate in the ineffective drainage subgroup (28.5%) was higher than that in the effective drainage subgroup (9.3%) ( p < 0.05). Bile bacterial culture was positive in 28 patients (71.8%), with the main pathogenic bacteria being Escherichia coli (15 cases) and Klebsiella pneumoniae (8 cases). Comparison of infection indicators before and after operation After PSM matching, in both the PTGBD and LC groups, all postoperative infection indicators, including C-reactive protein (CRP) and white blood cell count (WBC), were significantly lower than those before operation (all p < 0.05) (Table ). Correlation analysis showed that the reduction amplitude of infection indicators was positively correlated with the degree of clinical symptom improvement (reflected by the decrease in VAS pain scores) in patients of both groups (all p < 0.05) (Table ). Comparison of complications Using the Clavien-Dindo classification system, we standardized the definition, diagnostic criteria and detailed management measures for all complications in both groups, with results summarized in Table . PTGBD group: Complications occurred in 5 patients (12.8%), including 2 cases of Grade I (1 accidental catheter dislodgement, 1 catheter obstruction), 1 case of Grade II (catheter-related infection), and 2 cases of Grade III (bile leakage requiring interventional treatment). No Grade IV or V complications were observed. LC group: Complications occurred in 7 patients (17.9%), including 1 case of Grade I (incisional infection), 3 cases of Grade II (intra-abdominal infection improved with antibiotic therapy), and 3 cases of Grade III (1 postoperative acute cerebral infarction with partial neurological function recovery after conservative treatment; 1 bile leakage and 1 intra-abdominal hemorrhage, both requiring interventional treatment). No Grade IV or V complications were noted. No statistically significant difference was found in the overall complication rate between the two groups ( p > 0.05). Long-term follow-up The completion rate of 6-month long-term follow-up was 95.4% (166/174). Kaplan-Meier analysis showed that the 6-month recurrence rate in the PTGBD group (11.8%) was significantly higher than that in the LC group (1.7%) ( p < 0.05), while there was no statistically significant difference in the survival rate between the two groups ( p > 0.05) (Fig. ). Among the 25 patients with long-term catheter placement in the PTGBD group, 3 cases developed catheter-related complications (1 case of accidental catheter dislodgement,1 cases of infection and 1 case of obstruction), and 3 cases experienced cholecystitis recurrence. In the LC group, 4 cases developed long-term complications (2 cases of chronic abdominal pain and 2 cases of digestive dysfunction). Discussion‌ ACC is a life-threatening emergency that occurs frequently in elderly individuals [ , ]. Due to the common perception of geriatric patients as physically frail, along with their higher risk of complications and compromised physiological capacity, surgeons are often hesitant to select ELC as the primary treatment for their acute cholecystitis [ , ]. Compared with younger people, elderly patients are also prone to having a greater burden of comorbidities, with cardiovascular and respiratory disorders being particularly prevalent. Despite these unfavorable factors, multiple retrospective investigations that analyzed and compared perioperative outcomes of cholecystectomy between elderly and younger patients have indicated the absence of statistically significant differences in such outcomes [ – ]. Compared with younger people, elderly patients are also prone to having a greater burden of comorbidities, with cardiovascular and respiratory disorders being particularly prevalent. Despite these unfavorable factors, multiple retrospective investigations that analyzed and compared perioperative outcomes of cholecystectomy between elderly and younger patients have indicated the absence of statistically significant differences in such outcomes [ – ]. Such conflicting data makes managing ACC in elderly patients more challenging, forcing clinicians to strike a delicate balance between achieving effective disease control and minimizing the potential risks associated with treatment. When choosing treatment plans for this specific group of patients, extra caution is required—clinicians must balance effective disease control against the patients’ physical endurance and postoperative recovery potential. While many clinicians consider PTGBD more appropriate for elderly ACC patients, this treatment lacks high-quality clinical evidence. PTGBD can lead to various complications, such as pneumonia, sepsis, long hospital stays, catheter slippage, high mortality, the need for reoperation and other general complications [ ]. In contrast, LC is recognized as a relatively safe intervention and is recommended as the first-line therapy for ACC. Even so, LC is not entirely risk-free: relevant studies have demonstrated that this surgical approach is associated with a mortality rate of 0.3–0.5% and a bile duct injury rate of 0.2–1.5% [ , ]. The risk of major complications from LC increases with age, such as sepsis, acute lung failure, acute myocardial infarction, and acute stroke [ , ]. Due to underlying comorbidities, many elderly patients may lack the physical capacity to tolerate surgical intervention, and delaying surgery may be necessary. For elderly patients with high surgical risk, PTGBD is recommended as a safer alternative therapy to ease acute inflammation, and cholecystectomy can be carried out after their overall physical condition improves. The “3-day window period” has traditionally been regarded as the optimal timeframe for performing emergency cholecystectomy. However, recent studies suggest this window may be extended to 7 days or even up to 10 days after symptom onset [ , ]. Some scholars argue that during ACC, the gallbladder wall exhibits congestion, edema, and increased tension. Interestingly, edema within the loose connective tissue of the gallbladder wall may facilitate easier dissection, as adhesions to surrounding tissues are less dense and complex, preserving the anatomical integrity of Calot’s triangle and minimizing intraoperative bleeding. Our clinical experience, supported by the outcomes of the 121 patients in the ELC group, aligns with this observation: during ELC for acute cholecystitis, the edematous and thickened tissues provide a relatively clear surgical plane. By following this plane, bleeding is reduced, and the risk of gallbladder perforation (and subsequent bile spillage) is minimized—an advantage that is particularly critical in octogenarians, for whom even minor intraoperative complications can lead to prolonged recovery or severe adverse events. Notably, no perioperative deaths and bile duct injury occurred in the ELC group, and complications were limited to 7 cases. This low complication rate and absence of perioperative mortality underscore the feasibility and safety of LC in surgically fit octogenarians, even in the context of acute inflammation.​. Surgeons’ reservations about operating during acute inflammation often stem from concerns about obscured surgical fields due to severe adhesions, which increase the risk of bile duct injury [ ]. However, based on our practice and the outcomes of the present study, for most patients in the ELC group, adhesions during acute cholecystitis could be safely dissected with straightforward techniques, avoiding complex maneuvers. In cases of severe inflammation with obscured Calot’s triangle, we prioritize mobilizing the gallbladder from the gallbladder fossa before addressing Calot’s triangle—a strategy that further reduces the risk of iatrogenic injury and ultimately contributed to our 0.0% bile duct injury rate in early surgery performed by senior surgeons.​ ‌This finding aligns with conclusions from multiple high-quality clinical studies: Martino et al. [ ] demonstrated that ELC is as safe as elective surgery in elderly ACC patients with good surgical tolerance. Similarly, Budişcă et al. [ ] confirmed that early surgery can effectively reduce the occurrence of severe complications such as gallbladder perforation, noting that the risk of bile duct injury can be well controlled under standardized operation—findings that are consistent with our own experience of strict adherence to surgical protocols. When bile duct injury is suspected, intraoperative cholangiography via the cystic duct is performed [ ]; this precautionary measure further contributed to the low rate of major biliary complications observed in our LC cohort. Postoperative recovery metrics provide additional insights into the relative benefits of ELC versus PTGBD. A large case-series study published in 2017 reported that patients with Charlson co-morbidity index score (CCI) 6 or BMI 20 are at higher mortality risk if they undergo emergency cholecystectomy. If patients with jaundice (TBil 2.0 mg/dl), respiratory failure or neurological dysfunction are classified into Grade III on the severity grade of acute cholecystitis, PTGBD is recommended as the first choice in these high-risk patients rather than early or emergency surgical treatment [ ]. The results of our study showed significant differences between the two groups in the time to ambulation, time to first flatus, postoperative fasting time, length of hospital stay, and VAS pain score on the first postoperative day. These findings indicate that PTGBD is associated with faster recovery of gastrointestinal function and earlier ambulation, with less trauma to the body and better postoperative comfort—key factors in reducing the risk of postoperative complications such as deep vein thrombosis and pneumonia in elderly patients, which are highly prevalent in this population. Earlier ambulation and recovery of gastrointestinal function can also improve patients’ postoperative comfort and quality of life, which is particularly important in patients aged ≥ 80 years. Analysis of perioperative infection markers further supports the superior efficacy of ELC in controlling acute inflammation in elderly patients. Both the PTGBD and ELC groups demonstrated postoperative reductions in WBC count and CRP level, which are key markers of systemic inflammation closely associated with disease severity and clinical outcomes. However, the magnitude of decrease in these inflammatory indicators was significantly greater in the ELC group. These findings indicate that surgical removal of the diseased gallbladder provides more effective and definitive control of the underlying infection and systemic inflammatory response compared with temporary PTGBD drainage. In the present study, we further confirmed that the magnitude of reduction in WBC and CRP levels was positively correlated with the degree of pain relief as measured by VAS score. The stronger decrease in inflammatory markers in the ELC group was therefore consistent with more effective resolution of abdominal pain and faster clinical improvement. For patients aged 80 years and older, persistent systemic inflammation may aggravate pre-existing comorbidities and delay postoperative recovery. In this context, the advantage of ELC in achieving rapid and complete inflammation control carries important clinical implications for this vulnerable population. The relatively weaker reduction in inflammatory markers in the PTGBD group can be explained by its therapeutic mechanism, which only relieves gallbladder pressure without resecting the pathological focus. We speculate that potential reasons include residual biliary microlithiasis, delayed resolution of the systemic inflammatory response, insufficient drainage, or persistent occult infectious foci that cannot be eliminated by drainage alone. Taken together, changes in WBC and CRP levels not only reflect the degree of infection control but also closely parallel the improvement of clinical symptoms, further supporting ELC as a more reliable strategy for acute inflammation control in suitable elderly patients. The World Society of Emergency Surgery (WSES) guidelines recommend ELC as the standard treatment for elderly patients with comorbidities [ ] (e.g., heart disease, renal insufficiency, liver cirrhosis) when feasible. The 2018 Tokyo Guidelines [ ] advise ELC for surgically tolerable acute cholecystitis patients (regardless of symptom duration) and routine LC for select Grade III cases under strict criteria. The Chinese Guidelines for the Diagnosis and Treatment of Acute Biliary Tract Infections (2021) emphasize individualized risk assessment: ELC for mild cases, and surgery after general condition optimization for moderate-severe cases. Consistent with these, our results confirm ELC is safe and effective for patients aged ≥ 80 years with acute cholecystitis, even without strict adherence to the traditional 3-day window. PTGBD is a recommended temporary measure to control infection and reduce gallbladder tension, especially in high-risk patients unresponsive to antibiotics [ , ]. Its key limitation is lack of radicality (no gallbladder resection). While PTGBD can bridge to LC, studies show PTGBD plus delayed LC is safer and more effective than initial LC alone [ , ]. Conversion to delayed surgery varies: a multicenter randomized trial reported 29% (20/68) of PTGBD patients underwent subsequent cholecystectomy [ ], compared to 52.8% (28/53) in our study. In our PTGBD group, 47.2% (25/53) opted for long-term drainage; additionally, 5.7% (3/53) had post-discharge accidental catheter dislodgement, 3.8% (2/53) developed catheter-related infection, and 5.7% (3/53) experienced cholecystitis recurrence. The high long-term drainage rate in the PTGBD group highlights a major flaw: retaining the diseased gallbladder increases risks of cholecystitis recurrence and catheter-related complications (e.g., dislodgement, infection), and requires long-term medical management. For patients aged ≥ 80 years, long-term drainage also impairs quality of life and adds care burden. Thus, radical LC is preferable when clinically feasible. This study supplemented subgroup data of high-risk patients with ASA grade ≥ 4. Among 14 such patients, the success rate of PTGBD reached 100% with a complication rate of 28.6%, consistent with findings from similar studies [ ]. These results confirm the important application value of PTGBD in high-risk populations, addressing the limitation of previous studies that excluded this group. Additionally, propensity score matching (PSM) was used to balance baseline characteristics between the two groups, and sensitivity analysis verified the stability of the results, reducing the impact of selection bias on the conclusions. Long-term follow-up data showed that the LC group was significantly superior to the PTGBD group in terms of recurrence rate and quality of life, providing key evidence for the long-term value evaluation of treatment regimens. This study still has several limitations. First, although PSM reduced selection bias, the retrospective study design cannot completely eliminate it. Second, the sample size was relatively limited, especially in the PTGBD group, which may have affected statistical power. Finally, some long-term follow-up data were lost to follow-up, which may have had a slight impact on the results. Future studies should conduct large-sample, multicenter prospective randomized controlled trials to further verify the conclusions. In summary, compared with ELC, PTGBD has advantages in gastrointestinal function recovery, early ambulation, postoperative pain, and length of hospital stay, while ELC is more effective in inflammation control and long-term prognosis. For patients aged ≥ 80 years with acute calculous cholecystitis who can tolerate general anesthesia, ELC is the more ideal treatment option. In contrast, for high-risk surgical patients, PTGBD can serve as a safe and effective bridging therapy or long-term intervention. Clinical decisions should be made based on comprehensive assessment of individual patient conditions to optimize treatment efficacy and safety.

documents.title: Tokyo Guidelines 2018 Management of Acute Cholecystitis

chunks.content: Introduction Gallbladder stones account for approximately 80% of cholelithiasis cases, with about 15% of patients with gallbladder stones having concomitant common bile duct stones [ ]. With the continuous advancement of minimally invasive techniques, the combined application of laparoscopy, choledochoscopy, and duodenoscopy can essentially address most clinical cases of gallbladder stones combined with common bile duct stones [ – ]. Current treatment approaches can be categorized into two main strategies: endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) with stone extraction followed by laparoscopic cholecystectomy (LC), and laparoscopic common bile duct exploration (LCBDE) with stone extraction followed by LC. Both approaches share the common features of minimal trauma and rapid recovery, yet each has distinct characteristics. ERCP + LC may require a staged procedure, potentially disrupt Oddi sphincter function, and cannot completely avoid complications associated with endoscopic sphincterotomy (EST) performed during ERCP stone extraction; although with technological advancements, some centers employ balloon dilation of the Oddi sphincter as an alternative to EST, thereby avoiding sphincter injury [ ]. LCBDE + LC can be further subdivided into two approaches: laparoscopic trans-ductal common bile duct exploration (LTDBDE) and laparoscopic trans-cystic common bile duct exploration (LTCBDE). Both approaches allow for single-stage surgery and preservation of Oddi sphincter function. Previous literature reports that LTDBDE is associated with longer operative times and risks such as postoperative bile duct stenosis and bile leakage [ ]. With the ongoing development of fiberoptic choledochoscopy technology and continuous improvement in laser lithotripsy equipment, LTCBDE is being increasingly adopted in clinical practice [ – ]. With the continuous development of endoscopic techniques and the concept of “super minimally invasive” surgery [ ], many scholars tend to favor the ERCP + LC approach for managing common bile duct stones with gallbladder stones [ ]. For patients with common bile duct stones and acute cholangitis, ERCP offers a short operative time for stone removal, allowing prompt relief of obstruction. This staged surgical approach lays the groundwork for subsequent LC [ ]. For many elderly patients with multiple comorbidities, the stepwise treatment strategy of ERCP + LC is more easily accepted by patients and their families. This study found that the ERCP + LC group required more single-use consumables. Furthermore, as ERCP procedures at our institution are performed by the Department of Gastroenterology, ERCP + LC treatment often involves inter-departmental transfers and two separate surgical sessions. Our comparison revealed that the LTCBDE + LC group had a significantly shorter hospital stay ( P < 0.01) and lower total cost ( P < 0.01). Additionally, compared to the ERCP + LC group, LTCBDE + LC avoids sphincterotomy or T-tube placement. The trans-cystic approach can reduce postoperative management complexity and lower the long-term risk of bile duct stenosis, findings consistent with related studies [ , ]. In clinical practice, we are also exploring intraoperative collaboration between departments for same-session ERCP + LC to reduce the number of anesthetic episodes and lower treatment costs.The LTCBDE + LC approach holds more advantages. By treating both conditions in a single surgical session, it saves medical costs and consumables, benefiting both the healthcare system and patients. At our center, LTCBDE + LC is often the preferred surgical treatment for patients with gallbladder stones combined with common bile duct stones. This study found that the total operative time was shorter in the ERCP + LC group. The average operative time for LTCBDE reported by other domestic centers is (90.13 ± 20.36) minutes [ ]. The longer operative time for LTCBDE in our study may be related to it being in its initial stages at our center and the relatively small sample size. Although ERCP + LC has a shorter operative time, it increases the risk of post-ERCP pancreatitis [ – ]. Despite the longer operative time for LTCBDE + LC, the total hospital stay is shorter. LTCBDE + LC explores the common bile duct through the natural orifice (cystic duct), eliminating the need to incise the common bile duct or the Oddi sphincter, thereby preserving its physiological structure intact. This completely avoids duodenal perforation and reduces the incidence of bile reflux pancreatitis and cholangitis [ – ]. In contrast, ERCP + LC requires papillary sphincterotomy or dilation. Although some centers use balloon dilation as an alternative to mitigate injury, there remains a potential risk of functional impairment [ ]. In our clinical practice, we have found that an Fr11 or Fr9 single-use imaging catheter inserted via the cystic duct, guided by a guidewire, can smoothly enter the duodenum, allowing for complete biliary tract exploration via dilation and preventing missed stones. Particularly for young and middle-aged patients with common bile duct stones, the LTCBDE + LC approach offers more significant long-term benefits. The more significant reduction in transaminase levels in the ERCP + LC group may be related to the fact that ERCP stone extraction during the first stage promptly relieves biliary obstruction and decompresses the biliary tract, allowing for rapid bile drainage. This aspect makes it particularly suitable for patients in poor general condition who cannot tolerate prolonged surgery. Previous studies have identified the most common complications for both surgical approaches, including bile leakage, pancreatitis, cholangitis, intra-abdominal infection, biliary hemorrhage, duodenal perforation, and retained stones [ – ]. In this study, the case of worsened postoperative infection in the LTCBDE + LC group was attributed to excessive biliary pressure during surgery. During LTCBDE, the choledochoscope almost occupies the entire cystic duct lumen. If a common bile duct stone is tightly impacted and irrigation pressure is relatively high, biliary pressure can become elevated before obstruction is relieved, potentially leading to bile reflux into the bloodstream and exacerbating infection [ ]. Subsequent measures we adopted include: (1) Thorough dilation of the cystic duct to at least allow entry of a 5-mm laparoscopic dissector jaw, ensuring a sufficiently wide channel; (2) Using a 9 F (3 mm) or 11 F (3.7 mm) electronic choledochoscope with a smaller diameter, which leaves a gap for irrigation fluid egress, preventing excessive intrabiliary pressure; (3) Using warm saline for choledochoscopic irrigation, connected to an irrigation pump for pressure control; (4) Strictly limiting choledochoscopic stone extraction time (< 1.5 h); (5) Requiring the assistant to promptly aspirate saline and bile overflow during stone extraction; a drainage tube can also be pre-placed in the foramen of Winslow to allow timely outflow of irrigation fluid. Through these optimizations, no further cases of postoperative biliary tract infection occurred in subsequent surgeries in this study. The incidence of post-ERCP pancreatitis is approximately 9.7% [ ]. Its mechanism is not entirely clear but may involve factors such as repeated cannulation attempts, thermal injury during sphincterotomy, compression of the pancreatic duct orifice by dilation balloons impairing pancreatic juice drainage, or parenchymal injury from contrast or guidewires [ ]. At our center, for difficult cannulation, we routinely employ the double-guidewire technique. Studies show this method achieves a cannulation success rate of 88.6%, and pancreatic duct stent-assisted transpancreatic sphincterotomy can achieve a success rate of up to 97.1% [ ]. The case of bile duct perforation in the ERCP + LC group in this study was considered to be due to an impacted stone at the cystic duct terminus. Local impaction can cause inflammatory edema and fragility of the duct wall. Even under direct vision with a peroral cholangioscope, perforation of the cystic duct or common bile duct is highly possible. Some teams have reported cholangioscopy-assisted extraction through a papillary support for small common bile duct stones [ ], but strict adherence to indications and operative standards is crucial. Literature reports a retained stone rate after ERCP ranging from 4.8% to 14.9% [ – ]. For patients in the ERCP + LC group with common bile duct stones accompanied by multiple small gallbladder stones, finding residual stones via nasobiliary tube cholangiography post-ERCP is a viable option. Our center’s experience in avoiding retained stones during LTCBDE + LC includes: (1) Prevention: Preoperative MRCP clarifies stone number. Intraoperatively, fully secure the patient and adjust to a 45° head-up tilt to prevent stone migration into intrahepatic ducts. Control irrigation pressure after the choledochoscope enters the common bile duct. (2) Routine exploration of the common hepatic duct and proximal segments: Methods for intraoperative routine exploration of the common hepatic duct and left/right secondary hepatic ducts include: 1) Perform retrograde cholecystectomy to the cystic duct root, fully dissect the cystic duct root to clarify its junction anatomy. 2)Utilize the small diameter and four-way tip deflection of the electronic choledochoscope to advance it into the common hepatic duct and left/right hepatic ducts. 3) Occasionally, laparoscopic instrument assistance or splitting the cystic duct to its root may be needed to adjust the scope for retrograde advancement. 4) In some patients where the cystic duct has a low junction, joins the opposite wall of the common bile duct, or forms a very acute angle, making upward exploration impossible, intraoperative C-arm fluoroscopic cholangiography can be chosen to rule out retained stones, converting to laparoscopic transductal common bile duct exploration if necessary. Study limitations This study is a single-center retrospective analysis with a relatively small sample size (only 29 cases in the LTCBDE + LC group), which may affect the generalizability of the results. Furthermore, there is a lack of long-term follow-up data, particularly regarding the long-term benefits of preserving Oddi sphincter function. Future research should involve multicenter, large-sample randomized controlled trials, combined with cost-effectiveness analyses, to clarify the optimal indications for each technique. Additionally, advancements in ultra-slim choledochoscopes and laser lithotripsy technology may further optimize the efficiency of LTCBDE [ ], warranting continued attention. Of course, ERCP + LC remains safer and more effective for patients with severely inflamed common bile duct stones. Conclusion In conclusion, LTCBDE + LC demonstrates significant advantages in terms of minimal invasiveness, cost-effectiveness, and functional preservation, making it suitable for patients with appropriate cystic duct anatomy. ERCP + LC is more applicable for cases requiring rapid obstruction relief or where technical conditions are limited. We believe both approaches have their respective strengths and weaknesses but are equally safe and effective for treating gallbladder stones combined with common bile duct stones. On the other hand LTCBDE + LC is not without limitations. The procedure requires advanced laparoscopic skills, a steep learning curve, and access to specialized equipment such as pancreaticobiliary imaging catheter. In contrast, ERCP + LC is more widely available and may be more feasible in centers with limited laparoscopic expertise or resources. Therefore clinical decision-making should integrate individual patient characteristics, available medical resources, and surgeon experience to achieve precise treatment.

chunks.content: 1. Introduction Biliary tract diseases comprise a diverse group of benign and malignant disorders affecting the biliary ductal system and gallbladder [ , ]. Benign conditions, such as acute and chronic cholangitis, cholelithiasis, and biliary strictures, are common and contribute significantly to global morbidity and hospital admissions [ , ]. In contrast, malignant diseases, including cholangiocarcinoma and gallbladder cancer, are less prevalent but are often diagnosed at advanced stages, leading to poor prognosis and a significant clinical burden [ ]. Differentiating between benign and malignant biliary diseases remains challenging owing to overlapping clinical features, including jaundice, abdominal pain, and systemic inflammatory signs [ ]. Early and accurate diagnosis is essential to guide appropriate treatment strategies and improve patient outcomes. However, conventional diagnostic tools, such as ultrasonography, computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP), and standard laboratory tests, often demonstrate limited sensitivity and specificity. These limitations are particularly evident in early-stage disease or when distinguishing malignant from benign biliary strictures [ , ]. The growing emphasis on precision medicine has accelerated the development of novel diagnostic approaches that prioritize speed, accuracy, and personalized care. Point-of-care (POC) testing refers to diagnostic assays performed at or near the site of patient care and can deliver rapid, clinically actionable results, which are especially valuable in acute and outpatient settings [ , , ]. Concurrently, advances in molecular diagnostics have led to the identification of a wide range of biomarkers, including protein markers such as carbohydrate antigen 19-9 (CA19-9) and carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA), nucleic acids such as circulating microRNAs (miRNAs) and cell-free DNA, and various metabolites detectable in serum, bile, or tissue [ , ]. These biomarkers offer promising potential for early detection, improved risk stratification, prognostication, and treatment response monitoring in both benign and malignant biliary diseases [ ]. Moreover, artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning algorithms are increasingly being integrated with imaging and biomarker data to enhance diagnostic performance. These technologies can improve pattern recognition, support risk prediction, and enable individualized clinical decision-making pathways based on multimodal data sources and are set to revolutionize the diagnostic landscape [ , , ]. Despite these advancements, significant unmet needs remain, including the validation and standardization of emerging diagnostics, demonstration of clinical utility in diverse populations, and resolution of practical barriers to implementation in real-world settings. This review presents a comprehensive overview of current and emerging roles of POC testing and biomarkers in the clinical management of biliary tract diseases. It examines their diagnostic and prognostic applications, highlights recent technological innovations including AI-assisted tools, and discusses key research priorities and implementation challenges in this rapidly evolving field. 2. Epidemiological and Clinical Overview of Biliary Tract Diseases 2.1. Epidemiology and Clinical Burden Biliary tract diseases encompass a wide spectrum of hepatobiliary disorders that collectively contribute to significant global morbidity and healthcare resource utilization ( ) [ ]. Gallstone disease is highly prevalent worldwide, affecting both Western and Asian populations, and frequently leads to complications such as acute cholecystitis and ascending cholangitis [ ]. Although malignant biliary diseases, including cholangiocarcinoma and gallbladder carcinoma, occur less frequently, they are associated with markedly higher mortality rates, primarily due to their insidious onset, nonspecific clinical presentations, and frequent diagnosis at advanced stages [ , ]. Several risk factors predispose individuals to biliary tract malignancies. Chronic cholestasis, primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC), choledochal cysts, hepatolithiasis, and prolonged biliary inflammation have all been consistently associated with increased cancer risk [ , ]. Notably, the clinical and radiological overlap between benign inflammatory conditions and malignant transformations often complicates diagnosis, posing a substantial challenge in clinical practice. 2.2. Diagnostic Challenges in Clinical Practice The symptoms of biliary tract diseases are often nonspecific and overlap significantly between benign and malignant etiologies. Common presentations, such as abdominal pain, jaundice, pruritus, fever, and weight loss, lack adequate discriminatory value when considered individually. Although conventional imaging techniques, including transabdominal ultrasound, CT, and magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP), form the cornerstone of anatomical assessment, their capacity for functional or molecular characterization of lesions remains limited. Similarly, standard laboratory tests measuring liver enzymes, bilirubin, and inflammatory markers often suffer from low specificity, particularly in patients with coexisting liver dysfunction or systemic inflammation [ , ]. Thus, these diagnostic tools frequently fail to distinguish malignant strictures or tumors from benign inflammatory or obstructive processes, underscoring the need for improved diagnostic accuracy. 2.3. Unmet Needs in Biliary Diagnostics Given the limitations of current diagnostic workflows, there is an urgent need for tools that deliver rapid, reliable, and noninvasive diagnostic information at the point of care. Ideally, such approaches would enable early detection of biliary tract diseases, support accurate risk stratification, and facilitate timely therapeutic decision making. Point-of-care testing and molecular biomarker profiling have emerged as promising adjuncts to conventional imaging and laboratory evaluations. Point-of-Care Testing in Biliary Tract Disease 3.1. Principles and Clinical Utility POC testing refers to diagnostic assays conducted at or near the site of patient care that can deliver results within minutes. Such testing facilitates immediate clinical decision making by circumventing delays associated with centralized laboratories. In the context of biliary tract disease, this is particularly valuable during acute presentations, such as suspected cholangitis or biliary sepsis, where timely diagnosis and intervention can significantly reduce morbidity and mortality [ ]. A spectrum of POC technologies, ranging from bedside biochemical panels and inflammatory markers to advanced molecular diagnostics and real-time on-site cytological assessments, is either commercially available or under active clinical investigation for biliary tract disease [ , ]. An integrated diagnostic algorithm summarizing their clinical applications is illustrated in . summarizes the available and emerging POC modalities, their clinical utility, turnaround times, and limitations. 3.2. Current Point-of-Care Applications 3.2.1. Liver Enzyme and Function Panels Handheld or bedside analyzers capable of measuring liver enzymes such as alanine aminotransferase (ALT), aspartate aminotransferase (AST), alkaline phosphatase (ALP), gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT), bilirubin, and albumin are now commercially available and widely used in emergency departments and hospital wards ( ). These tools enable rapid triage and risk stratification of patients presenting with jaundice, abdominal pain, or suspected biliary obstruction. For example, in an emergency setting, elevated direct bilirubin and ALP levels from a bedside POC analyzer may prompt urgent imaging or consultation for potential ERCP [ ]. 3.2.2. Inflammatory and Infectious Markers POC assays for markers such as C-reactive protein (CRP) and procalcitonin are increasingly utilized for the diagnosis and monitoring of bacterial cholangitis and the assessment of infection severity [ ]. Some modern systems include automated leukocyte (white blood cell, WBC) and differential counts [ ]. For instance, a combination of elevated CRP levels and WBC counts may reinforce the suspicion of acute ascending cholangitis and justify the prompt initiation of antibiotics and biliary decompression. 3.2.3. Bedside Ultrasound POC ultrasonography (POCUS) has become a cornerstone for the rapid assessment of patients with suspected biliary diseases [ ]. Internists and gastroenterologists now frequently use handheld ultrasound devices to detect gallstones, biliary duct dilation, and gallbladder wall thickening and to assess complications such as abscesses or pericholecystic fluid. When incorporated into early clinical workflows, POCUS facilitates expedited diagnosis and intervention, particularly in unstable or critically ill patients. However, its sensitivity is operator-dependent and may be reduced in patients with obesity or excess bowel gas. Although POC tools and novel biomarkers are increasingly incorporated into practice, major international guidelines continue to differ in their diagnostic recommendations for biliary tract diseases [ ]. provides a comparative summary of key guidelines from the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases (AASLD), European Association for the Study of the Liver (EASL), Asian Pacific Association for the Study of the Liver (APASL), and the Tokyo Guidelines 2018, and it highlights opportunities for integrating POC testing and biomarker strategies into established diagnostic frameworks [ , , , ]. Across current international guidelines, diagnostic pathways remain focused on conventional clinical, biochemical, and imaging approaches. While AASLD and EASL mention CA19-9 (with or without CEA) as supportive markers in suspected cholangiocarcinoma, they stop short of recommending novel biomarkers. APASL guidelines emphasize early ERCP in obstructive cholangitis, reflecting regional disease patterns, but provide little guidance on biomarker use. The Tokyo Guidelines 2018 prioritize clinical and laboratory criteria for acute cholangitis severity assessment, without incorporating biomarkers. Overall, none of the guidelines formally recommend POC testing or novel biomarkers, highlighting a consistent gap between technological advances and clinical guideline integration. This underscores the urgent need for multicenter validation and consensus to incorporate POC testing and biomarker strategies into standardized biliary disease management. 3.2.4. The integration of ROSE, in which a cytopathologist or trained technologist assesses specimen adequacy and provides a preliminary diagnosis during the procedure, enables real-time feedback to the endoscopist [ ]. Rapid On-Site Evaluation (ROSE) Endoscopic ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration (EUS-FNA) is an established method for sampling masses and strictures of the bile duct and adjacent structures [ , ]. The integration of ROSE, in which a cytopathologist or trained technologist assesses specimen adequacy and provides a preliminary diagnosis during the procedure, enables real-time feedback to the endoscopist [ ]. This approach facilitates adjustments in the target site, needle type, or number of passes, increasing the diagnostic yield and often obviating the need for repeat procedures [ ]. Multiple studies have shown that ROSE during EUS-FNA improves diagnostic accuracy, shortens the time to a definitive diagnosis, and reduces unnecessary additional procedures in patients with indeterminate biliary strictures or suspected malignancy [ , , ]. In settings without on-site cytopathology, alternatives, such as telecytology and rapid staining kits, are under investigation [ ]. Limitations include the need for specialized personnel and workflow implications. Nevertheless, ROSE is increasingly reflected in clinical practice guidelines for optimizing tissue acquisition in biliary tract and pancreatic neoplasms. 3.3. Emerging Molecular POC Technologies The frontier of POC diagnostics has advanced rapidly with the advent of microfluidic devices, biosensors, and nucleic acid amplification technologies [ , ]. These platforms can detect bacterial DNA, viral RNA, and cancer-specific somatic mutations in minuscule volumes of blood, bile, or urine, potentially enabling pathogen identification or early cancer detection within an hour [ ]. While still under investigation, several pilot studies demonstrate their utility—such as PCR-based identification of causative bacteria in septic cholangitis [ ], or lab-on-a-chip mutation panels for rapid detection of common cholangiocarcinoma mutations (Kirsten rat sarcoma viral oncogene homolog (KRAS), isocitrate dehydrogenase 1 and 2 (IDH 1/2), fibroblast growth factor receptor 2 (FGF2), tumor protein p53 (TP53)) [ , ]. Portable miRNA chips also show promise for distinguishing malignant from benign strictures but require further clinical validation and standardization before widespread adoption. 3.4. Limitations and Practical Considerations While POC tests offer clear advantages in biliary disease management, including rapid results and support for timely decision making, several limitations must be considered. First, the accuracy of many POC assays may be lower than that of central laboratory methods, with variable sensitivities and specificities [ ]. This limitation can lead to occasional false-positive or false-negative results, making clinical interpretation and confirmatory testing essential. Operational challenges also persist. POC devices require regular calibration and staff training to ensure reliability. Lack of experience or poor technique may affect validity, particularly for operator-dependent tools such as POC ultrasound [ ]. The cost of purchasing, maintaining, and supplying consumables for POC equipment can be a significant barrier, especially in resource-limited environments where funding and reimbursement are uncertain. In addition, workflow integration remains challenging. Incorporating POC results into existing clinical protocols and electronic health records is not always seamless, and additional steps may complicate busy clinical settings [ ]. Furthermore, although novel POC technologies—such as molecular and genetic assays—show promise, their widespread adoption requires further validation in larger studies. Ultimately, POC tests should complement rather than replace comprehensive diagnostic assessments. Clinicians must interpret results in context and confirm findings with standard laboratory or imaging studies when appropriate. 4. Biomarkers in Biliary Tract Disease 4.1. Clinical Significance and Role of Biomarkers Biomarkers are quantifiable indicators of biological processes, pathological states, or response to therapy that are measurable in blood, bile, tissue, or other body fluids. In biliary tract diseases, they are increasingly central to early diagnosis, risk stratification, prognostication, and monitoring of treatment response. Effective biomarkers help differentiate benign from malignant processes, anticipate disease progression, and detect recurrence earlier than imaging or clinical symptoms. Their use is expanding alongside precision-medicine strategies ( ). 4.2. Established Serum Biomarkers 4.2.1. Carbohydrate Antigen (CA19-9) CA19-9 is the most widely used serum biomarker for cholangiocarcinoma and pancreatic cancer [ , ]. Its clinical utility is limited by suboptimal specificity, as levels may be elevated in obstructive jaundice, cholangitis, or pancreatitis, and by false negatives in Lewis antigen-negative individuals (approximately 5–10%), who do not synthesize the antigen [ ]. 4.2.2. Carcinoembryonic Antigen (CEA) CEA is sometimes measured in combination with CA19-9, but its low sensitivity and specificity, and its elevation in multiple benign and malignant conditions, restrict its value as a standalone test in biliary tract cancers [ ]. 4.2.3. Cholestatic Enzymes (ALP and GGT) Alkaline phosphatase and GGT are classic indicators of cholestasis; however, they cannot reliably distinguish between malignant and benign biliary diseases [ ]. 4.3. Circulating- and Bile-Derived miRNAs Circulating and bile-derived miRNAs, notably miR-21, miR-221, and members of the miR-200 family, are stable in body fluids and show disease-specific upregulation in cholangiocarcinoma [ ]. Importantly, current international guidelines do not yet incorporate miRNA-based assays into diagnostic pathways, underscoring the need for rigorous validation before clinical implementation. Nevertheless, these markers represent promising candidates for future integration into guideline-based biliary disease management once reproducibility and real-world applicability are confirmed. 4.3.2. This approach is promising for early detection, molecular profiling, and selection of targeted therapies. For example, in a study by Rizzo et al., a ctDNA panel demonstrated a specificity of approximately 93%, though sensitivity was variable and generally lower in early or low-tumor-burden cases [ ]. Other reports have similarly indicated that sensitivity often ranges between 50–70% for key driver mutations in plasma samples, reflecting the challenges of tumor heterogeneity and low mutant allele frequency in early disease [ ]. Importantly, most existing studies are limited by small sample sizes and retrospective design, and multicenter prospective trials are required to confirm real-world clinical utility. While validation is ongoing, liquid biopsy approaches may supplement or, in select scenarios, substitute for tissue-based diagnostics. 4.3.4. Emerging Serum Protein Biomarkers Emerging protein candidates, including leucine-rich α-2-glycoprotein (LRG), osteopontin, and pyruvate kinase M2 (PKM2), show diagnostic and prognostic potential. Machine learning models, such as EfficientNet, applied to 3D refractive index tomograms have demonstrated excellent diagnostic performance, with reported AUC values exceeding 0.99 in distinguishing cancerous from normal cholangiocytes in experimental studies [ ]. Beyond simple classification, visualization techniques (e.g., LayerCAM) consistently highlight lipid droplet-rich regions that correspond to known cancer-associated metabolic phenotypes. Although these findings are highly promising, current evidence remains limited to preclinical and small-scale translational studies. Many candidates still lack large, prospective, multicenter validation in demographically and etiologically diverse cohorts with prespecified clinical endpoints. Utility is further limited by reliance on invasive sampling (e.g., ERCP-derived bile), variable costs and reimbursement, and the operational challenges of embedding results into clinical workflows and electronic health records. Technological Innovation Recent advances in microfluidics, biosensors, and lab-on-a-chip platforms are enabling rapid, multiplexed diagnostics deployable at the bedside and, increasingly, in the home. These integrated approaches have the potential to surpass traditional diagnostics by improving accuracy, enabling real-time risk stratification, and supporting point-of-care clinical decision making. 5.2. Second, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and harmonization efforts should establish optimal biomarker panels, assay methodologies, and clinically actionable thresholds to facilitate standardization and comparability across institutions. Third, clear regulatory and reimbursement pathways are required to support safe, sustainable implementation through robust quality assurance and post-market performance monitoring. Finally, incorporating patient-reported outcomes and quality-of-life measures into clinical evaluations will clarify the broader impact of early diagnosis and minimally invasive monitoring. chunks.content: Introduction Percutaneous transhepatic gallbladder drainage (PTGBD) is widely performed to control inflammation prior to emergency surgery in patients with acute cholecystitis [ ]. In cases of severe acute cholecystitis, current guidelines recommend initial management with PTGBD, followed by laparoscopic cholecystectomy (LC) once the patient’s general condition has stabilized, rather than proceeding directly to emergency surgery [ , ]. However, the optimal timing of LC after PTGBD remains controversial. Some studies advocate early surgery [ – ], while others suggest that delayed surgery may be more beneficial [ – ]. From a surgical perspective, LC following PTGBD can remain technically challenging. Although PTGBD effectively alleviates acute inflammation, residual inflammatory changes, dense adhesions, and fibrotic distortion of anatomy around Calot’s triangle are frequently encountered [ , ]. Both excessively early surgery (performed before sufficient resolution of inflammation) and excessively delayed surgery (associated with progressive fibrosis and adhesions) may increase operative difficulty. These opposing pathophysiological processes suggest that the relationship between surgical timing and operative difficulty may be inherently non-linear rather than monotonic. In such situations, surgeons may be forced to perform bailout surgery, including conversion to open surgery, subtotal cholecystectomy, or alternative dissection strategies such as a fundus-first approach, to avoid major bile duct injury [ , ]. Previous studies evaluating the timing of cholecystectomy after PTGBD have several methodological limitations. Surgical timing has often been categorized using arbitrary cutoff values, and potential non-linear associations between timing and surgical difficulty have not been adequately assessed. Moreover, few studies have specifically focused on bailout surgery as a clinically meaningful indicator of intraoperative technical difficulty [ ]. We hypothesized that the relationship between the interval from PTGBD to LC and the requirement for bailout surgery would not be strictly linear. This is because operative difficulty may initially decrease as acute inflammation resolves after drainage, but may subsequently increase due to the development of fibrosis and adhesions. Therefore, the primary objective of this study was to evaluate whether the interval from PTGBD to LC, treated as a continuous variable, is associated with the probability of bailout surgery, and to explore whether a clinically relevant temporal threshold can be identified using restricted cubic spline modeling. Methods This retrospective observational study was conducted at Kishiwada Tokushukai Hospital. All patients who underwent cholecystectomy at the institution between November 2014 and November 2024 were retrospectively reviewed. Patients diagnosed with acute cholecystitis were identified according to the Tokyo Guidelines 2018 (TG18). Among these patients, those who underwent LC following PTGBD were eligible for inclusion in the study. At our institution, the decision to perform PTGBD was not based solely on TG18 severity grading. Although PTGBD was routinely performed in TG18 severe cases, additional clinical and logistical factors were considered. Patients receiving oral anticoagulant therapy (including direct oral anticoagulants and warfarin) were generally managed with PTGBD prior to definitive cholecystectomy. Antiplatelet therapy alone was not regarded as an indication for PTGBD. In cases of concomitant common bile duct stones and acute cholangitis requiring endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP), PTGBD was frequently performed to control gallbladder inflammation while endoscopic treatment was prioritized. Therefore, such cases were considered part of the real-world post PTGBD population and were included in the analysis. Patients with suspected or confirmed gallbladder malignancy were not identified in this cohort. No cases of concomitant acute pancreatitis were observed. Additionally, PTGBD was occasionally selected when emergency laparoscopic cholecystectomy could not be promptly performed due to temporary unavailability of surgeon capable of emergency biliary surgery. Such situations included nighttime hours, weekends or public holidays, and periods during which the surgical team was engaged in other operative procedures. In these circumstances, the decision between surgery and PTGBD was made at the discretion of the attending physician rather than based on a fixed institutional protocol. The primary outcome was the requirement for bailout surgery during LC. Secondary outcomes included operative time, intraoperative blood loss, postoperative length of stay, and the occurrence of major postoperative complications, defined as Clavien–Dindo grade ≥ III. Bailout surgery was defined as any of the following intraoperative procedures: conversion to open surgery, subtotal cholecystectomy, or the use of a fundus-first approach. At our institution, LC is routinely initiated with an approach from the gallbladder neck. The standard surgical technique involves confirmation of the critical view of safety, followed by division of the cystic artery and cystic duct, and subsequent dissection of the gallbladder from the liver bed. A fundus-first approach was defined as initiation of gallbladder dissection from the fundus prior to identification and control of the cystic structures. As most continuous variables demonstrated non-normal distributions, they are presented as median and interquartile range (IQR) and were compared using the Mann–Whitney U test. The interval from PTGBD to LC was treated as a continuous variable. Because the biological course of inflammation resolution and subsequent fibrotic remodeling after PTGBD is unlikely to follow a strictly linear trajectory, restricted cubic spline (RCS) modeling was used to flexibly evaluate potential non-linear associations between surgical timing and outcomes. These outcomes were strictly positive in the study cohort, with no zero values observed. Given their right-skewed distributions and the presence of a small number of extreme values, gamma regression with a log link was considered appropriate to model multiplicative effects while reducing sensitivity to extreme observations. Exponentiated coefficients from gamma models are interpreted as ratios of expected means, representing multiplicative effects on the outcome scale. From a clinical and surgical standpoint, residual pathological changes following PTGBD may provide a more plausible explanation for operative difficulty than elapsed time alone. Although PTGBD effectively alleviates acute inflammatory symptoms, local pathological alterations, including persistent edema, dense adhesions, fibrotic remodeling, and distortion of the anatomy around Calot’s triangle may evolve heterogeneously among patients. These changes can obscure anatomical landmarks, limit safe dissection, and increase the risk of bile duct injury, thereby necessitating bailout procedures including subtotal cholecystectomy, conversion to open surgery, or a fundus-first approach. Consequently, a predefined interval from PTGBD to LC may not accurately reflect the intraoperative conditions encountered at cholecystectomy. In this context, the independent association between CRP level at diagnosis and the requirement for bailout surgery is clinically informative. CRP may serve as a more direct and objective indicator of inflammatory burden than elapsed time, which is only an indirect proxy for the underlying pathological process. This finding suggests that inflammatory markers at presentation may provide more actionable information for anticipating operative difficulty than relying on the interval from PTGBD to LC alone. In addition to bailout surgery, we evaluated several secondary outcomes reflecting operative burden and postoperative recovery. The interval from PTGBD to LC was not independently associated with operative time or intraoperative blood loss. Although a statistically significant association was observed for postoperative length of stay, the estimated effect size was very small. The magnitude of this association was minimal, corresponding to an approximate 0.7% increase in postoperative length of stay per additional day in the PTGBD to LC interval, which is unlikely to be clinically meaningful. These findings suggest that, within the observed timing range, elapsed time alone did not substantially influence procedural complexity or resource utilization. Furthermore, no independent association was observed between surgical timing and major postoperative complications (Clavien–Dindo grade ≥ III), indicating that the absence of a temporal threshold was consistent across both technical and patient-centered outcomes. These findings should be interpreted in the context of current guideline recommendations for acute cholecystitis. Contemporary guidelines advocate early laparoscopic cholecystectomy for many patients with mild-to-moderate disease and recommend gallbladder drainage as a bridging strategy in selected high-risk or severe cases. The present study does not address the initial decision between early surgery and drainage but rather examines scheduling after PTGBD has already been performed. Within this post-drainage context, we did not identify a clear time-based threshold associated with reduced operative difficulty. Because most procedures in our cohort were performed within approximately 30 days after PTGBD, the present analysis cannot exclude the possibility that different associations might emerge at longer intervals; however, within the timing range observed in this cohort, no clear temporal threshold associated with reduced operative difficulty was identified. Overall, these findings suggest the need for caution in applying rigid recommendations on the timing of LC after PTGBD. This pragmatic design, reflecting heterogeneous real-world clinical decision-making, represents a key strength of the present study. Rather than relying on elapsed time alone, surgical decision-making may benefit from an integrated assessment of inflammatory status, clinical course after drainage, radiologic findings, and intraoperative judgment. A flexible, patient-centered strategy integrating inflammatory markers and clinical trajectory after drainage may therefore be preferable to a fixed time-based interval. An important consideration when interpreting these findings is that the present cohort represents a heterogeneous real-world institutional decision population rather than a strictly guideline-driven PTGBD cohort. A substantial proportion of patients with mild and moderate acute cholecystitis also underwent PTGBD in our cohort. This reflects real-world institutional practice in which PTGBD may be selected for reasons other than TG18 severity alone, including anticoagulant therapy, the need to prioritize ERCP for concomitant bile duct stones or cholangitis, and temporary logistical constraints related to surgeon availability. To address this potential selection bias, we performed a sensitivity analysis restricted to TG18 mild and moderate cases, which demonstrated findings consistent with the primary analysis. Therefore, the present findings should not be interpreted as evidence against the clinical relevance of surgical timing after PTGBD in guideline concordant populations, but rather as observations derived from a heterogeneous real-world cohort in which the indication for PTGBD itself was variable. This suggests that the absence of a clear temporal association in the present study is unlikely to be solely explained by heterogeneity in patient selection, although such effects cannot be completely excluded. Indications for PTGBD at our institution were determined based on clinical judgment rather than strict protocolized criteria, and therefore may not fully reflect guideline-driven practice patterns. Consequently, the study population represents a real-world institutional cohort rather than a standardized severity-based PTGBD population, which may affect generalizability. In addition, although the study period spanned 10 years, a strong cumulative learning-curve effect at the primary-operator level may be attenuated in our institutional setting. Acute cholecystitis cases are predominantly performed by residents within a relatively narrow postgraduate-year range under direct supervision of attending surgeons, while senior surgeons more frequently assume supervisory roles rather than serving as primary operators. As a result, the operative experience of the primary surgeon may have remained relatively consistent throughout the study period. Nevertheless, temporal changes in perioperative management or institutional practice patterns cannot be entirely excluded. Second, bailout surgery was used as a pragmatic surrogate marker of intraoperative technical difficulty. Although conversion, subtotal cholecystectomy, and fundus-first approaches are widely accepted safety strategies, their implementation may vary according to surgeon experience and institutional culture. Therefore, the threshold for bailout procedures may not be universally applicable. Third, although restricted cubic spline modeling allowed flexible assessment of potential non-linear associations, estimates at the extremes of the PTGBD to LC interval were less precise due to limited sample size in those ranges, as reflected by widening confidence intervals. Although the number of events was moderate relative to the number of covariates included in the multivariable model, the model complexity was limited and the consistency of findings across sensitivity analyses supports the robustness of the results. Finally, detailed radiologic severity features such as gallbladder wall thickness, pericholecystic fluid, or abscess formation were not systematically evaluated and therefore were not included in the analysis. Although TG18 severity grading incorporates clinical and laboratory parameters, unmeasured imaging characteristics may have influenced intraoperative difficulty. In addition, surgeon-level factors and longitudinal changes in inflammatory status after drainage were not incorporated into the present analysis. Future prospective, multicenter studies integrating standardized imaging findings, objective measures of operative complexity, and surgeon-related variables are warranted to more comprehensively determine how surgical timing should be integrated into decision-making after PTGBD. Conclusions In this single center real-world retrospective cohort of patients with acute cholecystitis undergoing laparoscopic cholecystectomy after PTGBD, the interval from drainage to surgery was not independently associated with the probability of bailout surgery when modeled as a continuous variable using restricted cubic splines. Within the observed timing range in this cohort, no clear time-based threshold was identified for reducing the likelihood of bailout surgery. These findings suggest that elapsed time alone may be insufficient to guide surgical timing after PTGBD, and that individualized clinical assessment may better inform operative planning. Although a small association with postoperative length of stay was observed, the magnitude of this effect was minimal.
